column1: # PB-SEC-4 -- WITHDRAWN AND INVERTED. The app allows screenshots; this is what that exposes.
# ADR-007 B65, ruled by the owner on 2026-07-26: the shipped app permits screenshots and screen
# recording. FLAG_SECURE and setRecentsScreenshotEnabled(false) are gone from
# dev.swarm.phone.SecureWindow, and every row below therefore reads false in both columns.
# THE TABLE SURVIVES THE DECISION IT NO LONGER RECORDS THE OPPOSITE OF, and that is the point.
# Deleting it would leave nothing behind; keeping it inverted keeps the one property the
# original bought -- that this is a DECISION and not drift -- and keeps the record of what the
# decision COSTS, screen by screen, where the next person to argue about it will look.
# android/gate/s18_sec4_windowsecurity_test.go enforces both halves: no production Kotlin may
# name FLAG_SECURE or setRecentsScreenshotEnabled, and every row here must read false.
# Reinstating the flag fails that gate, which is how the next re-add -- for what will feel at
# the time like an obvious security improvement -- is made to read B65 first.
# WHY, IN SHORT. The protection was a compositor HINT: not attested, no defence against a camera
# pointed at the screen, and no defence against an accessibility service, which reads the
# rendered screen regardless (android/input-path-limits.md). So it stopped an app that could
# already screenshot and stopped nothing else. Against that it blocked users of a DEVELOPER TOOL
# from sharing terminal output, which is an ordinary thing to want from this product.
# WHAT IS RENDERED TODAY AND WHAT IS NOT, stated plainly so this table is not read as a claim
# about a finished app. S18 delivers a MINIMAL Activity (the amended PB-SEC-4 ruling), and
# PhoneSurface renders two of the rows below: the pairing surface and the terminal peek, which
# are the two the requirement named. The rest exist as S16 screen models with no view attached
# yet. They are listed because the decision is what this artifact records, and because they
# inherit it by construction when they land: there is ONE window and nothing is set on it. A
# later surface that needs different treatment has to argue for it in this file -- and it now
# has to argue against B65 rather than merely fill in a row.
# flag_secure          false: the compositor is not asked to refuse screenshots or screen
#                      recording for the window.
# exclude_from_recents false: setRecentsScreenshotEnabled(false) is not called, so the system
#                      writes the ordinary recents thumbnail when the app backgrounds. Stated
#                      separately from flag_secure because they were separate decisions and are
#                      separately re-addable; B65 withdrew both.
# WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE. Session content is still sealed at rest (S15) and still kept out of logs
# (PB-SEC-3); gated controls still filter obscured touches (PB-SEC-12 clause 1, untouched by
# B65). Those are the layers that survive device loss, which is the threat they were written
# against. What a screenshot needs is an adversary already executing on the unlocked handset.
# Columns: screen <TAB> flag_secure <TAB> exclude_from_recents <TAB> why
pairing
column4: Named by the withdrawn requirement, and the row that carried the sharpest argument: it shows the SAS emoji the person compares against their machine's screen, so a screenshot of it hands an interceptor the one value the comparison exists to protect. ANSWERED, not overwritten: the SAS is live only for the seconds of a ceremony bounded at 60 s, the comparison is made against a screen the owner is looking at, and an attacker positioned to screenshot the handset mid-ceremony has already defeated the ceremony's premise. A narrowing of margin, recorded as such, not the removal of a control.

column1: session_detail
column4: NAMED BY THE WITHDRAWN REQUIREMENT'S ARGUMENT, WHICH IT INHERITED FROM THE TERMINAL PEEK. That row is deleted with its screen (ADR-009-structured-chat-interaction (3)), and the argument it carried is not: this screen shows the session's conversation -- what the agent said, what it ran, what it changed -- which is the same session content PB-SEC-3 keeps out of logs and S15 seals at rest, in a more legible form than the grid it replaces. Allowing screenshots undoes one layer of that ONE LEVEL UP. ANSWERED, in the peek's own words because the answer is unchanged: the layers below survive device loss, which is the threat those requirements were written against, and a screenshot needs an adversary already executing on the unlocked handset. It is also the screen the decision exists for -- sharing what an agent did is what a developer tool is for. The journal half of the old row still holds: it names sessions and their state.

column1: triage_inbox
column4: The roster: session titles, groups and the one-line need summary. Individually less than a grid, collectively a map of what the owner is working on, and a title is often the most sensitive line on screen. That is the cost of the decision on this screen, stated rather than dropped; it is accepted for the same reason as the peek, and a screenshot of it needs the same adversary.

column1: machine_pane
column4: Presence, the paired device, the activity log, and the two gated controls (revoke, kill switch state). The activity log is journal content under another name. Its controls keep their own defence: filterTouchesWhenObscured is PB-SEC-12 clause 1 and B65 does not touch it.

column1: settings
column4: Push preferences and the handset's biometric-gate preference. No session content. It was protected because it was hosted by the same window, and it is unprotected now for exactly the same reason: there is one window, and an exception would have to be argued rather than inherited.

column1: connection_banner
column4: Not a screen but a surface on every one of them, listed so its coverage is recorded rather than assumed. It renders the connection state, including the terminal "revoked" and "repair required" verdicts. Nothing on it is secret from someone holding the unlocked handset, which is the only adversary a screenshot serves.
